identity.title: Abdominojugular (hepatojugular) reflux: sustained JVP rise >3 cm with 10-30 s abdominal pressure

technique.how: With the patient reclined so the top of the jugular column is visible and breathing normally through an open mouth, apply firm steady mid-abdominal pressure with the flat hand for 10-15 s (up to 30 s) while watching the neck. Positive if the column rises and stays up >=3-4 cm for the duration of compression and then drops abruptly on release.
technique.prerequisites: Visible internal jugular column at baseline (adjust bed angle first); patient must avoid Valsalva or breath-holding.
technique.contraindications: Painful or acute abdomen, recent abdominal surgery, or inability to breathe normally during compression.

interpretation.positive_finding: Sustained rise (>=3-4 cm, >=10 s) indicates the right heart cannot accept the extra venous return: elevated right atrial pressure, and in left heart failure a wedge pressure of roughly >=15 mm Hg.
interpretation.negative_finding: A transient rise that falls back within a few heartbeats is normal and argues against elevated right-sided filling pressure and against congestion in a patient whose resting JVP is borderline.
interpretation.pitfalls: Valsalva, breath-holding, or abdominal guarding during compression gives a false positive; too little pressure or too short a compression gives a false negative. Isolated RV failure (e.g., RV infarct) can be positive without high wedge pressure.
interpretation.changes_what: Positive reflux confirms venous congestion and supports HF/RV failure and diuresis; negative with a normal resting JVP lowers probability of congestion.

estimates.population: 65 adults considered free of heart failure undergoing routine cardiac catheterization; positive test = sustained jugular rise >=1 cm
estimates.reference_standard: Right heart catheterization (mean right atrial pressure)
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 1.0/(1-0.85) = 6.67 from abstract sensitivity 1.0 and specificity 0.85; LR- not computed because sensitivity of 1.0 gives an unstable 0 in n=65
estimates.quote: A positive test had high sensitivity and specificity for predicting right atrial pressure greater than 9 mm Hg (1.0, 0.85)

estimates.target_condition: Right ventricular end-diastolic pressure >12 mm Hg
estimates.population: 65 adults considered free of heart failure undergoing routine cardiac catheterization; positive test = sustained jugular rise >=1 cm
estimates.computed_from: LR+ = 0.90/(1-0.89) = 8.18; LR- = (1-0.90)/0.89 = 0.11, from abstract sensitivity 0.90 and specificity 0.89 (no CIs in abstract)
estimates.quote: right ventricular end-diastolic pressure greater than 12 mm Hg (0.90, 0.89)

sources.citation: Sochowski RA, Dubbin JD, Naqvi SZ. Clinical and hemodynamic assessment of the hepatojugular reflux. Am J Cardiol. 1990;66(12):1002-1006.
Ewy GA. The abdominojugular test: technique and hemodynamic correlates. Ann Intern Med. 1988;109(6):456-460.
Wang CS, FitzGerald JM, Schulzer M, Mak E, Ayas NT. Does this dyspneic patient in the emergency department have congestive heart failure? JAMA. 2005;294(15):1944-1956.
Cook DJ, Simel DL. The Rational Clinical Examination. Does this patient have abnormal central venous pressure? JAMA. 1996;275(8):630-634.

safety_scope.do_not_use_when: Do not perform with an acute or tender abdomen, fresh laparotomy, or when the baseline jugular column cannot be seen (result is uninterpretable, not negative).
safety_scope.escalation_warning: A positive reflux with hypotension or a new murmur suggests RV infarction, massive PE or tamponade; obtain ECG/echo urgently rather than diuresing empirically.
safety_scope.interobserver_note: Bedside observation agreed well with the catheter-measured response in the same patients (kappa 0.74, Sochowski 1990); reproducibility across examiners in undifferentiated dyspnoea is not established.

extraction_notes: Wang 2005 (PMID 16234501) pools hepatojugular reflux for ED heart failure but the LR is not in the abstract and no open-access full text exists, so the pooled estimate is not recorded. Sochowski 1990 estimates come from a non-heart-failure catheterization cohort using a >=1 cm threshold, not the >=3 cm threshold in this record's title; treat as evidence the sign tracks right-sided pressure, not as ED diagnostic accuracy. Ewy 1988 (PMID 3415106) defines the standard technique (10 s firm midabdominal pressure, >=3 mm Hg / 4 cm rise then abrupt fall) and reports mean PCWP 19 vs 10.5 mm Hg for positive vs negative tests but no sens/spec, so no estimate entered. Marantz 1990 (Am J Cardiol) could not be located in PubMed search.
